title: Post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage
subtitle: Every bleed is admitted; a child hides blood loss until late

sources.org: American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery Foundation (AAO-HNSF)
sources.title: Clinical Practice Guideline: Tonsillectomy in Children (Update)

sources.org: Royal College of Surgeons of England and British Association of Otorhinolaryngologists
sources.title: Key messages from the National Prospective Tonsillectomy Audit (Laryngoscope 2007)
Tranexamic acid and beyond: a systematic review of pediatric post-tonsillectomy hemorrhage protocols and introduction of a universal management guideline (Casey et al.)

red_flags.text: Any fresh blood from the mouth or nose after tonsillectomy, however small. A small 'herald' bleed often precedes a large one.
Frequent swallowing, especially in a sleeping child: the child is swallowing blood.
Vomiting of dark or altered blood. The stomach can hold a large volume before anyone sees it.
Tachycardia, pallor, cool peripheries or prolonged capillary refill in a child. Hypotension is a late, pre-arrest sign.
Clot sitting in the tonsil fossa: it is holding a bleeding vessel open and will bleed again.
Airway compromise from blood or clot, or a reduced conscious level.

do_now.text: Sit the patient up and forward, or lie a drowsy child on their side. Ask them to spit, not swallow. High-flow oxygen.
Call the senior ENT surgeon and the senior anaesthetist now, for any active bleeding, not after the bloods return.
Intravenous access (two cannulae if possible), full blood count, coagulation tests, and group and crossmatch.
Nil by mouth from now, because the next step may be an anaesthetic with a stomach full of blood.

assess.text: Estimate the blood loss against the child's circulating volume, not the adult's. A few hundred millilitres is a large proportion of a small child's blood volume.
Look in the mouth with a good light and suction: active bleeding, clot in the fossa, or a clean fossa with slough. Normal white slough is not infection.
Timing: primary haemorrhage within 24 hours is usually technical; secondary haemorrhage after 24 hours, typically days 5 to 10, is usually associated with infection or separation of slough.
Ask about poor oral intake, pain, fever and anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, and whether the operation used a hot technique.
Track the observations as a trend: heart rate, capillary refill and an early warning score every 15 minutes while bleeding.

investigate.text: Haemoglobin may be normal early in an acute bleed. Treat the clinical picture, not the first result.
Coagulation tests where there is a bleeding history, anticoagulant use, or a large or recurrent bleed.
No imaging is needed for a typical bleed. A massive or recurrent bleed in an unusual pattern may need CT angiography to look for vascular injury.

resuscitate.text: Fluid and blood resuscitation in proportion to the loss and the physiology, with early blood in a shocked child.
Intravenous tranexamic acid per local protocol: published protocols commonly include it for active bleeding.

Local measures in a cooperative patient who is not bleeding heavily: gentle removal of clot by suction, and topical vasoconstriction or hydrogen peroxide per local protocol, by an experienced clinician only.

definitive.text: Return to theatre for active bleeding not stopped by local measures, for a significant bleed with haemodynamic change, and for recurrent bleeding.

The anaesthetic is high risk: full stomach of blood, blood in the airway, and hypovolaemia. Senior anaesthetist, rapid sequence induction, two suction devices, a range of tube sizes, and the surgeon scrubbed before induction.
In theatre: identify the bleeding point, then control it with bipolar diathermy, ties or oversewing the pillars. Aspirate the stomach before waking the patient.
Admit every patient with a post-tonsillectomy bleed for observation, even if it has stopped by arrival, and treat with antibiotics per local protocol for a secondary bleed.
Record each haemorrhage and return to theatre for audit. The guideline recommends that surgeons know their own bleeding rates.

escalate.text: Senior ENT and senior anaesthetist for every active bleed. Paediatric anaesthesia and paediatric critical care for a child with haemodynamic compromise.
Ligation of the external carotid artery or embolisation is a last resort for uncontrolled bleeding, needing senior and interventional radiology input.

Units without an on-site ENT surgeon need a local agreement for stabilisation and transfer. A child bleeding at night is not transferred without a senior escort and a secured airway if bleeding is active.

notes: The sentinel bleed is the warning. Clinicians who send home a child with a small bleed that has stopped are relying on luck.
A child compensates with heart rate and vasoconstriction until they suddenly do not. Capillary refill and heart rate trend are the vital signs here, not blood pressure.
The National Prospective Tonsillectomy Audit found higher haemorrhage rates with hot techniques than with cold steel. Know which technique was used.
